title: Spatiotemporally controlled drug release via a click-release system utilizing mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine and cyclooctyne chemistry

paper_content.abstract: The advancement of bioorthogonal bond-breaking chemistry requires precise spatiotemporal control over chemical reactions. In this study, we introduce a click-release strategy based on the reaction between mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine and cyclooctyne (COT), enabling rapid and nearly complete payload release. We demonstrate that mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine and hydroxylamine react with COT to form nitrone and oxime, respectively, facilitating a versatile and efficient release mechanism. By conjugating mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine with responsive cleavable groups, we convert its inherent reactivity into an on-demand activation system. In vivo, this strategy is applied in a 4T1 mouse breast tumor model, showing significant tumor inhibition compared to the parent anticancer drug. Additionally, in local anesthesia, the anesthetic effect could be modulated by light exposure, allowing for repeated activation. This click-release system combines fast kinetics, high release efficiency, and precise spatiotemporal control, offering promising applications in chemical biology and drug delivery.
paper_content.introduction:
Click chemistry has fostered an unprecedented synergy between chemistry and biology, revolutionizing research paradigms in the life sciences through its exceptional reaction selectivity and efficiency1–6. Initially celebrated for its robust, bioorthogonal covalent bond formation, click chemistry has empowered precise biomolecule labeling, visualization, and manipulation within complex biological systems7–9. More recently, the advent of the click-release strategies—wherein a rapid click reaction is directly coupled to a subsequent bond-cleavage event—has expanded the toolkit for in situ payload liberation10–13, driving transformative implications in bioimaging14, regulation of the activity of nucleic acids and enzymes15–19, drug delivery20–26, and beyond27–30. In particular, the tetrazine (Tz)—triggered decaging of trans-cyclooctene (TCO)—caged molecules has attracted extensive attention owing to its extraordinary reactivity and biocompatibility31,32, fueling applications ranging from tumor imaging33,34 and immunomodulation35–37 to prodrug therapies38–43, one of which has advanced into phase II clinical trials44.

Despite these remarkable achievements, a critical need persists for bioorthogonal platforms that deliver not only rapid reaction kinetics and high release efficiency but also exquisite spatiotemporal control. The intrinsic always-on reactivity of traditional bioorthogonal handles limits their potential for precise activation and localization. Recent efforts—such as Wang’s concentration-promoted click—release strategy that enriches reactants at defined sites45, along with the methods reported by Devaraj46,47 and Pu34,48 that employ photo-controlled or enzymatic deprotection of dihydrotetrazine (DHTz) precursors to generate Tz—have begun to surmount these challenges. Despite these advancements, reported strategies remain relatively scarce and predominantly focus on modifications of the tetrazine scaffold. Consequently, the development of controllably activatable bioorthogonal reaction platforms remains highly desirable and represents a crucial frontier in the field.

In pursuit of a more versatile solution, recent work by Kim and colleagues has exploited the ring strain–promoted hydroamination of N,N-dialkylhydroxylamines with alkynes to generate N-oxides49 that can be reductively triggered by boron reagents50. Similarly, Ji’s group has accelerated decaging kinetics via silicon substitution in boronic acid systems, thereby enhancing prodrug activation51. Yet, the intrinsic instability and perpetual reactivity of boron reagents have hindered precise spatiotemporal modulation in complex settings.

In this work, we expand the chemistry of ring strain–assisted hydroamination by showing that mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine reacts directly with cyclooctyne (COT) to form a hydroxyaminooctene intermediate. When a leaving group is installed at the propargyl position of COT, this intermediate undergoes rapid 1,4-elimination, releasing the payload and generating a nitrone octene—a bioorthogonal bond-cleavage reaction with fast kinetics and near-quantitative efficiency (Fig. 1a). Capitalizing on the synthetic versatility of hydroxylamine, we developed a “caged” design in which its click activity is masked via a carbamate linkage. This dormant state can be activated by specific stimuli—elevated glutathione (GSH), enzymatic action, or light—enabling precise spatiotemporal control over the release process (Fig. 1b). The utility of this stimuli-responsive platform is demonstrated through two complementary in vivo applications: tumor-targeted prodrug activation triggered by the reductive tumor microenvironment in a 4T1 breast cancer model, and repeatable, on-demand local anesthesia controlled by 405 nm light. Together, these results establish a versatile click–release system for spatially and temporally controlled bioorthogonal chemistry (Fig. 1c).
paper_content.results:
Hydroxylamine and mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine hydroamination reactions with COT
Building on the proposed click-release platform design, we initially investigated the fundamental reactivity between hydroxylamine derivatives and COT. Our mechanistic hypothesis proposed that enamine N-oxides, formed via retro-Cope elimination between hydroxylamine and COT, could undergo proton transfer at the nitrogen center, yielding nitrone through N-alkyl-hydroxyl-enamine intermediates. Notably, this proton transfer requires a transferable proton on the hydroxylamine nitrogen—a feature inherently absent in N,N-dialkylhydroxylamines, which are restricted to enamine N-oxide formation (Fig. 2a,b).

To test this hypothesis, we systematically examined the reactivity of both mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine and hydroxylamine with COT, characterizing the resulting products. As expected, the initially formed N-oxides underwent proton transfer, leading to the production of nitrones and oximes, respectively (Fig. 2c). Quantitative analysis by HPLC revealed that when COT 1a reacted with mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine 2c in a mixed aqueous solution (50% ACN/PBS) at room temperature, 81% conversion was achieved within 30 min, reaching nearly 99% conversion after 2 h (Fig. 2d). In contrast, hydroxylamine 2a showed significantly lower reactivity under identical conditions, with only 41% conversion after 30 min (Fig. 2e). This reduced reactivity is attributed to the weaker nucleophilicity of hydroxylamine compared to its N-alkylated counterpart. The absence of alkyl substituents in hydroxylamine fail to sufficiently stabilize the nitrogen cation generated during retro-Cope elimination, thus increasing the activation barrier. Importantly, both hydroxylamine and mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine participated in reactions with efficiencies that meet stringent click chemistry criteria.

Expanding our investigation, we evaluated the hydroamination reactivity of a series of hydroxylamine derivatives with COT (Supplementary Fig. 1A-D). Given the ease with which mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine can be modified, we functionalized them with various groups at the nitrogen or oxygen positions. Our results revealed that modifications substituting the proton on the oxygen atom (compounds 2f and 2g) or sterically shielding the nucleophilic nitrogen (compounds 2h and 2i) completely abolished reactivity (Fig. 2f). Conversely, mono-alkyl-hydroxylamines bearing various alkyl substituents successfully reacted with COT 1a, yielding the corresponding click products. HPLC analyses demonstrated a clear correlation between steric parameters and reaction efficiency. Derivatives 2b and 2c, with minimal steric hindrance, exhibited the highest click reactivity, with over 80% conversion within 30 min. In contrast, increasing steric bulk progressively diminished the reaction rate, with compound 2a (lacking alkyl substitution) also exhibiting suboptimal reactivity. Notably, the tert-butyl substituted derivative 2e displayed the lowest click reactivity among those tested, with only 14.4 ± 2.9% conversion within 30 min (Fig. 2g).

Bioorthogonal mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine/COT bond-cleavage chemistry
Following the establishment of the reactivity of our click reaction, we focused on its potential application in triggered molecular release. As previously noted, the click reaction between mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine and COT results in the formation of an N-alkyl-hydroxyl-enamine intermediate. We hypothesize that this intermediate facilitates a spontaneous 1,4-elimination process upon introduction of a leaving group at the propargylic position, ultimately leading to the development of a bioorthogonal cleavage chemistry.

To validate this concept, we synthesized COT 3a using p-nitroaniline as a model caging molecule and examined its reaction with mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine 2c in a 20% ACN/PBS solution at room temperature. As expected, this reaction led to the successful release of p-nitroaniline, with a release yield of up to 97.9%. In contrast to the reduction of N-oxides formed from N,N-dialkylhydroxylamine and COT by boric acid to release caged molecules, our findings reveal that mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine can directly function as a bioorthogonal scissor to cleave caged molecules tethered to COT, eliminating the need for an additional reduction step (Fig. 3a,b).

To further validate this mechanism, we monitored the reaction progress using 1H NMR spectroscopy. To capture the reaction midpoint, we selected the less reactive mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine derivative 2e (Fig. 3c). Within 10 minutes of mixing 25 mM of substrate 3a with 50 mM of 2e in DMSO-d6, the formation of nitrone 3d was observed by 1H NMR spectroscopy, which captured the alkene proton generated from the elimination reaction (two addition isomers were observed), along with the quantitative release of the payload, p-nitroaniline (3c). As the reaction progressed, the gradual disappearance of 3a corresponded with the increasing release of p-nitroaniline. After 1 h, only trace amounts of 3a remained, and by 12 h, complete consumption of 3a was observed with full payload liberation. Notably, the elimination intermediate 3b was not detectable, suggesting that once formed, it rapidly eliminates to release p-nitroaniline. Furthermore, the absence of any non-releasing byproducts confirms the excellent regioselectivity of the click reaction, ensuring nearly complete payload release.

To further characterize the decaging chemistry, we conducted a systematic evaluation of both the reaction kinetics and substrate scope. A series of probes (4b and 4c), bearing representative nitrogen- and oxygen-based leaving groups, were synthesized via carbamoylation or Mitsunobu reactions. As anticipated, the fluorescence of both coumarin and naphthalimide was effectively quenched in these caged compounds (Fig. 4a). When incubated in PBS at 37 °C, neither 4b nor 4c exhibited any fluorescence over 1 day (Supplementary Fig. 2A, B), confirming their stability.

Upon testing the reactivity of 4b in a 20% DMSO/PBS solution at room temperature, we observed the rapid consumption of 50 μM 4b in the presence of 300 μM of hydroxylamine 2c. This reaction led to the formation of product 4d, accompanied by a significant increase in fluorescence intensity at 438 nm, and the formation of nitrone 4a (Fig. 4b). Quantitative HPLC analysis revealed that the disappearance of 4b was nearly stoichiometrically matched by the formation of 4d, achieving a release efficiency as high as 96% (Fig. 4c). The absence of detectable elimination intermediates further emphasizes the rapidity of the release process. By monitoring the time-dependent increase in fluorescence at 438 nm, we determined a rate constant (k2) of 1.8 ± 0.1 M−1s−1 at room temperature, which increased to 4.7 ± 0.1 M−1s−1 at 37 °C (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 3A, B).

Under similar conditions, probe 4c exhibited exceptional reactivity. In the presence of 2c, 4c was almost completely consumed within 10 minutes, releasing 4e and generating nitrone 4a (Fig. 4e). The corresponding fluorescence increase at 556 nm allowed us to calculate a rate constant of 39.1 ± 6.1 M−1s−1 (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 3C). Expanding this analysis to additional bond types, we synthesized 4f, which, upon treatment with 2c, was converted to nitrone 4g within 30 min, accompanied by the loss of a fluoride ion as confirmed by LC–MS (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Fig. 4). The rate constant for this reaction, monitored via the nitrone absorption peak at 300 nm, was determined to be 10.1 ± 1.0 M−1s−1 (Supplementary Fig. 5A, B).

These results confirm the robustness of our bioorthogonal bond-breaking chemistry, which efficiently cleaves a wider range of bonds, including carbamate, ether, and others. The elimination step occurs rapidly, with the overall release rate being primarily governed by the initial click reaction. Moreover, the high regioselectivity of the reaction between hydroxylamine and COT ensures near-complete payload liberation. Notably, payload-bearing COT derivatives show high stability against biologically relevant nucleophiles like glutathione (GSH), cysteine (Cys), and dimethylamine (DMA), as previously confirmed25.

Effectiveness of click-release strategy in cellular environments
Encouraged by our findings, we next validated the efficacy and bioorthogonality of our click–release strategy within cellular environments, applying it to both bioorthogonal fluorescence imaging and prodrug activation.

For fluorescence imaging, we first incubated 4T1 breast cancer cells with the caged probes 4b and 4c at a concentration of 20 μM for 60 min; under these conditions, no fluorescence signal was observed, confirming that the probes remain inert in the absence of a trigger. Following this, subsequent treatment with mono‑alkyl‑hydroxylamine 2c at 100 μM resulted in a pronounced increase in fluorescence—blue for 4b and green for 4c—as visualized by confocal microscopy (Fig. 5a,b). This result indicates that the ether and carbamate bonds in these probes are efficiently cleaved in the cellular milieu via the click–release mechanism, leading to robust activation of the fluorophores.

To extend the system for in vivo imaging applications, we synthesized compound 5a, designed to shift the emission to the near‑infrared (NIR) region (Fig. 5c). Compound 5a displayed effectively quenched fluorescence and remained non‑fluorescent when incubated in 20% DMSO/PBS at 37 °C for 24 hours (Supplementary Fig. 6). In contrast, when 5a was used at 50 μM in the presence of 2c at 250 μM, we observed a robust increase in fluorescence intensity at 620 nm, peaking within 1 h with a decaging rate constant (k2) of 3.1 ± 0.2 M−1s−1 (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Figs. 7, 8). Consistently, when 5a (20 μM) and 2c (100 μM) were co‑incubated with 4T1 cells, significantly enhanced red fluorescence was detected after 60 min (Fig. 5e), confirming efficient release of the NIR fluorophore. To further evaluate whether this click-release chemistry is sufficiently biocompatible to proceed within live cells, we synthesized COT-chloroalkane 5d (Supplementary Fig. 9A). 4T1 cells expressing HaloTag-PS were incubated with 5d (50 μM) for 1 h. After washing with PBS to remove extracellular 5d, the cells were treated with hydroxylamine 2c (100 μM) for 30 min. A significant increase in blue fluorescence was observed (Supplementary Fig. 9B, C), confirming not only the cell permeability of both reactants but, critically, their successful intracellular reaction.

Building upon these imaging studies, we applied the click–release strategy to bioorthogonal prodrug activation. Doxorubicin (DOX) was conjugated to cyclooctynol via a carbamate bond to generate the prodrug 5c, effectively masking its cytotoxicity. HPLC monitoring revealed that, upon treatment with 2c, 5c was rapidly consumed within 1 h, concomitant with the release of DOX. The click–release process proceeded with a rate constant of 4.8 ± 0.3 M−1s−1, and the overall release yield was determined to be 98.2 ± 0.7% (Fig. 5f,g and Supplementary Fig. 10A, B).

Finally, we evaluated the antiproliferative activity of prodrug 5c in combination with 2c using 4T1 cells. Mono‑alkyl‑hydroxylamine 2c alone was non‑toxic, even at concentrations up to 1 mM. In contrast, prodrug 5c alone exhibited markedly reduced cytotoxicity compared to free DOX. Importantly, when cells were co‑treated with 5c and 2c, the cytotoxic effect was effectively restored, with the inhibitory activity on cell proliferation approaching that of free DOX (Fig. 5h). This result strongly suggests that 5c is efficiently activated in the cellular environment via the click–release strategy.

Spatiotemporally controllable click-release chemistry
In Fig. 2f, we demonstrate that acylation of the nitrogen atom in mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine effectively shields its reactivity. Exploiting this property, we linked various responsive bond-breaking groups to hydroxylamine via carbamate bonds to block its clickability (i.e., Clickability OFF). Upon exposure to a specific stimulus, the blocked clickability is restored (Clickability ON), thereby enabling precise control over the timing and location of the click–release event. To this end, we developed a controlled activation strategy by designing and synthesizing three hydroxylamine derivatives with distinct activation mechanisms: thiol-responsive 6a, photo-activated 6b, and nitroreductase (NTR)-responsive 6c. In each case, the clickability of these compounds was effectively masked until triggered.

To demonstrate specificity, we first activated compound 6a by incubation with 2 mM glutathione (GSH) and subsequently performed a click reaction with probe 4b. Under these conditions, more than 98% of product 4d was released after 2 h, whereas in the absence of GSH, less than 5% of 4d was generated (Fig. 6a). Similarly, to verify that 6c could be activated, we treated it with an aqueous solution of sodium sulfite as a mild reducing agent. The results confirmed that the clickability of 6c was restored, thereby enabling the release of the caged 4d from COT 4b.

Given that endogenous GSH concentrations in cancer cells typically range from 1 to 10 mM—substantially higher than the extracellular levels in normal cells (generally below 10 µM)52—we investigated whether compound 6a could be activated by the GSH-rich milieu present in tumor cells. When 6a (100 µM) and probe 4c (10 µM) were incubated with 4T1 cells, confocal microscopy revealed prominent green fluorescence after 2 h, indicating successful activation. In contrast, pretreatment of cells with the thiol-reactive reagent N-ethylmaleimide (NEM) (500 µM for 1 h) to deplete endogenous GSH resulted in only weak fluorescence upon subsequent incubation with 6a and 4c (Fig. 6b).

To further validate the in vivo efficacy of our strategy, compound 6a and probe 5a were co-injected intratumorally into 4T1 tumor-bearing mice to assess GSH-triggered activation localized within the tumor microenvironment. Significant fluorescence was observed at the tumor site for over 7 h, whereas the control group that received only probe 5a exhibited no detectable fluorescence at any time point (Fig. 6c). These results suggest that the clickability of 6a is efficiently activated in the high GSH environment of tumor hypoxic regions, thereby turning on fluorescence via the click–release mechanism.

Building upon the successful demonstration of bioorthogonal imaging, we extended our strategy to prodrug activation to further showcase the versatility of our spatiotemporally controlled click–release system. Cytotoxicity assays in 4T1 cells confirmed the effectiveness of the approach: 6a alone shows no impact on cell viability, even at concentrations as high as 300 μM. Encouragingly, after its combination with 5c, the cytotoxicity exhibited a greater inhibitory effect on the cancer cell line than free DOX, indicating that this prodrug has been effectively activated within the cells (Fig. 6d and Supplementary Fig. 11). These results underscore the potential of our click–release strategy for precise, spatiotemporal control over prodrug activation in complex biological environments.

To illustrate that our strategy enables control not only over the reaction location via endogenous stimuli but also over the reaction timing via exogenous triggers, we evaluated the photo-activated system. Under 405 nm LED light, the clickability of compound 6b was activated, allowing it to react with probe 4b and achieve more than 98% release of product 4d after 100 min. In contrast, in the absence of light, only trace amounts of 4d were observed (Fig. 6e and Supplementary Fig. 12A-C). Moreover, when 6b and probe 4c were co-incubated with 4T1 cells, confocal microscopy revealed significant green fluorescence in the light-exposed group, whereas no fluorescence enhancement was observed in the group without light (Fig. 6f).

Overall, through simple chemical modification we effectively blocked the clickability of mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine and then reactivated it using specific stimuli—either endogenous (e.g., GSH, NTR) or exogenous (e.g., light). This spatiotemporally controllable click–release strategy thus offers precise regulation over the timing and location of molecular release, broadening its potential applications in targeted drug delivery and bioorthogonal imaging.

GSH-triggered bioorthogonal prodrug for targeted cancer treatment
To further validate the therapeutic potential of our spatiotemporally controlled click–release strategy, we evaluated its in vivo efficacy using a GSH-triggered bioorthogonal prodrug in a 4T1 mouse breast tumor model. Building on our encouraging in vitro results, 4T1 cells were subcutaneously implanted into mice, which were then randomly assigned into five groups (n=5 per group). Once tumor volumes reached 60–100 mm³ (typically after 7 days), treatment commenced with administrations every other day for a total of four injections.

For treatment, the prodrug 5c (2.4 mg/kg, DOX-equivalent) was pre-mixed with 6a (17 mg/kg) and administered via a single tail vein injection. In parallel, a positive control group received free DOX (2 mg/kg), while separate control groups were treated with 5c alone (2.4 mg/kg) or with PBS (100 μL). Throughout the experimental period, tumor growth and body weight were monitored daily until day 12. When the tumor volume in the PBS group approached 1500 mm³, the animals were euthanized, and tumors along with major organs were collected for analysis (Fig. 7a).

As illustrated in Fig. 7b,d, mice treated with 6a alone exhibited tumor growth comparable to that of the PBS group, and prodrug 5c by itself showed only a modest inhibitory effect. Notably, the combined administration of 5c and 6a resulted in a significant suppression of tumor growth, outperforming both the negative control and the free DOX group. Histological analysis via H&E staining also revealed that the tumor tissues from the group receiving the combination of 6a and 5c exhibited significantly higher levels of necrosis and apoptosis. Importantly, no significant changes in body weight were observed in any treatment group during the study period, demonstrating the safety of the strategy, which was further supported by H&E staining of the collected vital organs, including the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys (Fig. 7b-e and Supplementary Fig. 13).

To directly confirm that the bioorthogonal click–release reaction occurs at the tumor site, we conducted a pharmacokinetic (PK) study comparing free DOX (2.0 mg/kg) with a prodrug system consisting of compound 5c (2.4 mg/kg DOX equivalent) and the GSH-responsive activator 6a (17 mg/kg), both administered via intravenous injection. Doxorubicin concentrations in plasma, tumor, heart, and liver were quantified using UPLC-MS/MS at multiple time points. In contrast to free DOX, the 6a + 5c group showed markedly reduced drug levels in non-target tissues (e.g., heart and liver) and in the plasma, while maintaining comparable tumor concentrations across all time points (Supplementary Fig. 14). These results provide compelling evidence that the click-release reaction is preferentially triggered within the tumor microenvironment by elevated endogenous GSH, thereby effectively reducing off-target exposure. While this study establishes spatially selective prodrug activation in vivo, further validation in expanded cohorts and extended therapeutic studies will be essential to confirm long-term safety and efficacy.

Photo-triggered bioorthogonal prodrug for local anesthesia
In contrast to the GSH-activated system that relies on endogenous stimuli, this section explores the use of an exogenous trigger to demonstrate the conceptual versatility of our click–release strategy. As a proof-of-concept, we designed a photo-triggered prodrug system for local anesthesia. We note that the anesthetic effect could, in principle, be achieved through more straightforward direct uncaging approaches; however, the present design serves to illustrate the modularity of the platform and the decoupling of the activation trigger from the payload structure. In this system, the conventional local anesthetic tetracaine was conjugated to COT via a carbamate bond to mask its anesthetic activity, yielding the prodrug 7a. In vitro studies under 405 nm LED irradiation, in the presence of the photoactivator 6b, showed that 7a released tetracaine with an 89.4 ± 2.4% yield within 30 min (Fig. 8a).

To facilitate in vivo application, 7a and 6b were incorporated into a thermosensitive hydrogel formulation (P407-(6b+7a). This formulation remains liquid at room temperature for ease of injection and gels at body temperature, thereby prolonging drug retention at the administration site.

For in vivo evaluation, the P407-(6b+7a) formulation was injected into the plantar surface of rat paws. The local anesthetic effect was quantified by stimulating the footpad with a Touch Test sensory evaluator, with subsequent measurement of withdrawal responses to calculate the maximum peak effect (MPE) and duration of nerve block (see “Methods” for details). Notably, administration of 7a alone produced no anesthetic effect, confirming that the activity of tetracaine was effectively masked. However, upon exposure to 405 nm LED light 10 min post-injection, the prodrug was activated, yielding an anesthetic effect comparable to that of free tetracaine (Fig. 8b).

The anesthetic effect was further modulated by adjusting the light intensity and exposure duration. Irradiation at 200 mW cm−2 for 2 min produced a nerve block lasting 26.3 ± 7.5 min, while increasing the irradiance to 300 mW cm−2 extended the duration to 33.8 ± 7.5 min. Prolonging the exposure at 300 mW cm−2 to 5 min further extended the block to 48.8 ± 7.5 min (Fig. 8c).

To address clinical needs for prolonged pain relief, we also evaluated the potential for repetitive on-demand local anesthesia. After an initial light-triggered nerve block, subsequent exposures were administered once the previous effect had subsided. Over the course of five cycles, each exposure produced a measurable anesthetic effect (Fig. 8d); however, the duration of the block gradually decreased with successive triggers—likely due to drug depletion—with up to four effective activations observed (Fig. 8e).

To assess the safety of the drug delivery system, rats were euthanized at 4 and 14 days following the administration of free tetracaine, prodrug 7a, or the combination treatment (7a+6b). Footpads were harvested for subsequent histological analysis. Consistent with the known inflammatory responses associated with local anesthetic injections53, mild to moderate inflammation was observed in all treatment groups at day 4. By day 14, inflammation had largely resolved in all cohorts. Importantly, the 7a+6b combination group did not demonstrate exacerbated toxicity compared to the other treatment arms, thus supporting the favorable safety profile of this delivery system (Supplementary Fig. 15).

These findings collectively demonstrate that our photo-triggered bioorthogonal prodrug system provides precise temporal control over the delivery of local anesthetics using an exogenous light stimulus. This approach not only distinguishes itself from endogenous glutathione (GSH)-triggered systems but also presents a tunable method for on-demand pain management with potential clinical applications.

Chemical synthesis
Synthesis protocol and additional characterization can be found in the Supplementary Information.

HPLC monitoring of hydroamination between COT 1a and hydroxylamine
HPLC analysis: COT 1a (1 mM) and hydroxylamine (3 mM) were dissolved in 50% ACN/PBS, and the obtained solution was incubated at room temperature. An aliquot was taken from the mixture at intervals for HPLC analysis. The conversion was determined based on the HPLC data.

Reaction kinetics studies
The rate of this click-release reaction is almost entirely dependent on the rate of the first click step because the release step is too fast to monitor the intermediates. Therefore, the overall rate of click release was measured in this experiment.

Reaction progress was monitored either by the increase in fluorescence intensity (for payload release) or by the rise in UV absorbance (for nitrone formation). The conversion C at time t was calculated from the measured signal St as C = (St - S0) / (Smax - S0) where S0 is the initial baseline signal and Smax is the signal at reaction completion. The concentration of each reactant at time t was then determined as [A] = [A]₀(1–C) and [B] = [B]₀(1–C).

The second-order rate constant k was obtained by fitting the time-dependent concentration data to the integrated rate Equation 1.
kt = 1 / ([B]₀ - [A]₀) * ln ([A]₀[B] / [B]₀[A])
where [A]₀ and [B]₀ are the initial concentrations (mmol/mL), and t is the reaction time (s). The value of k is reported in M−1s−1.

Fluorescence-based monitoring (for 2c with COT derivatives 4b, 4c, and 5b): Stock solutions of hydroxylamine 2c and the corresponding COT derivative (50 mM in DMSO) were diluted with PBS to the desired PBS/DMSO ratio and final concentration, affording separate solutions of the COT derivative (solution A) and hydroxylamine 2c (solution B). Solutions A and B were rapidly mixed in equal volumes. After a brief initial delay, fluorescence intensity at the characteristic emission wavelength was recorded using a fluorescence spectrophotometer. Measurements were repeated at fixed time intervals until the signal reached a plateau. The kinetic trace (fluorescence intensity vs. time) was converted to concentration versus time as described above, and the second-order rate constant was extracted from the fit to equation (1).

UV-based monitoring (for 2c with COT 4f): Separate acetonitrile solutions of COT 4f and hydroxylamine 2c were prepared at the desired concentration. The two solutions were rapidly combined, and after a set delay, the UV absorbance at 300 nm was measured with a UV spectrophotometer. Absorbance readings were taken at regular intervals until no further increase was observed. The absorbance-time profile was converted to concentration-time data and fitted to equation (1) to obtain the second-order rate constant.

HPLC-based monitoring (for 2c with COT 5c): The release of doxorubicin (DOX) from COT 5c upon reaction with hydroxylamine 2c was quantified by HPLC. Aliquots withdrawn at designated time points were analyzed to determine the concentration of released DOX. The resulting release profile (Fig. 5f) was treated as described above, and the second-order rate constant was calculated from the fit to Eq. (1).

Stability assessment
Stability of fluorescent Probes 4b, 4c, and 5a: The stability of probes 4b, 4c, and 5a was evaluated by monitoring changes in their fluorescence intensity. Each compound was dissolved in 20% DMSO/PBS to a final concentration of 20 μM, and the solution was incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Fluorescence intensity at the characteristic emission wavelength of the parent fluorophore was recorded at 0 h and 24 h.

Fluorescence or HPLC‑based monitoring of stimulus‑triggered payload release from probe 4b
The release of payload 4d from probe 4b under various stimuli was monitored by fluorescence spectroscopy. Stock solutions (50 mM in DMSO) of the probe (4b) and each trigger compound (6a, 6b, or 6c) were prepared. Appropriate dilutions were made to obtain the desired working concentrations in a mixed solvent system. The release was initiated by combining the diluted solutions of probe 4b and the respective trigger compound.

For activation by glutathione (GSH), a 50 mM GSH stock solution in PBS was added to the mixture containing compound 6a to a final concentration of 5 mM. The reaction mixture was then incubated at 37 °C. For photo‑triggered release, the mixture containing compound 6b was directly exposed to 405 nm LED light at room temperature. For activation by sodium dithionite, a 50 mM Na2S2O4 stock solution in PBS was added to the mixture containing compound 6c to a final concentration of 5 mM, followed by incubation at 37 °C.

In all cases, payload release was verified either in real-time by tracking the fluorescence increase at 438 nm using a fluorescence spectrophotometer, or by quantitative HPLC analysis of samples taken at designated time points.

Preparation of P407-(6b+7a)
At 0 °C, dissolve 4 g of P407 in 16 mL of PBS to prepare a 20% P407 solution. Dissolve compound 7a in a small amount of ethanol, then add an equivalent molar amount of 2 M HCl. After completely removing the solvent by reduced pressure evaporation, the obtained 7a hydrochloride is dissolved in P407 aqueous solution. Next, it is mixed with an appropriate amount of 6b in DMSO solution to prepare a hydrogel formulation. The final concentrations are 50 mM for 7a and 60 mM for 6b, with 10% DMSO included. The formulation is typically stored at a temperature of 0–4 °C (it will form a gel at room temperature or 37 °C).

Cell culture
The 4T1 cells (Product No. CC-Y2004) used in this study were purchased from Shanghai EK-Bioscience Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium (Jiangsu Ketu Biotechnology Co., Ltd.; Cat. No. RG-CE-4) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2.

Cytotoxicity assay
4T1 cells in the logarithmic growth phase were seeded on 96-well plates at a density of 5 × 103 cells per well. Following a 24-h incubation at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 atmosphere, the cells were treated with the tested compounds at different concentrations for an additional 24 h. Subsequently, the cells were washed twice with PBS and treated with 10% CCK-8 (Keygen BioTECH; Cat. No. KGA1606-500) for 1 h at 37 °C. The absorbance at 450 nm was then recorded using a microplate reader. Cell viability was assessed by calculating the ratio of experimental wells (after subtracting background) to control wells (also after subtracting background).

Cell imaging studies
Briefly, after incubating 4T1 cells in a confocal culture dish for 24 h, the culture medium is replaced with a culture medium solution containing the desired concentration of the compound. After the set incubation time, stain with Hoechst 33342 for 10 minutes if needed. Then, detection and image capture are carried out using CLSM (Olympus Corporation, Japan).

Stable 4T1 cell lines expressing the HaloTag protein from the pHaloTag-PS plasmid (where PS denotes the HSV-TK poly(A) signal) were generated as follows. Briefly, 4T1 cells were seeded in 6-well plates at a density of 5.0 × 105 cells per well in 2 mL of RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100 units/mL penicillin, and 0.1 mg/mL streptomycin. Groups of SD rats were kept in an environment with a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle. reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The work describes a new kind of a cageable click to release system using cyclooctynes that react with caged hydroxylamines. In general, bioorthogonal chemistry can suffer from off target reactions, and so mechanisms to control where such reactions occur are needed. The work is thorough and should be of interest to the wider community. However, I found several issues that need to be addressed before being reconsidered for publication.

A major issue is the lack of certain controls. The mechanism of the release strategy relies initially on a nucleophilic attack of the COT by the hydroxylamine. This necessarily makes one question the biorthogonality and whether COT or the many COT derivatives react with biological nucleophiles like amines and especially thiols. Its actually well known that cyclooctynes can react with thiols and this leads to side reactions. Thus, it would be important for the authors to rigorously show how their caged COT derivatives respond to high concentrations of thiols and amines in physiologically relevant buffer conditions.

The imaging in Figure 5a and 5d can be of higher quality and could be magnified to make the details clearer. As it is now, its extremely unclear and blurry.

In the conclusions the authors should discuss the drawbacks and potential future direction for improvements of their technology. One drawback is the rate of reaction, which is lower than the faster tetrazine/TCO click to release reactions. Also, the use of very strong nucleophiles like hydroxylamines might have drawbacks in vivo as would the use of cyclooctynes which are known to undergo side reactions with thiols. Some more discussion here would be good. There are likely other areas for improvement that the authors may wish to discuss.

Minor points:
Regarding the statement “along with the methods reported by Devaraj and Pu that employ photocontrolled or enzymatic deprotection of dihydrotetrazine (DHTz) precursors to generate Tz—have begun to surmount these challenges.” The Devaraj lab has also described enzymatic uncaging in a preprint that was published before the work of Pu. I suggest the authors cite this work as well. See: https://chemrxiv.org/engage/chemrxiv/article-details/65b6ca2e9138d23161ee5b4e

Also, I’m not sure this is a fair comment: However, the necessity for the challenging synthesis and modification of tetrazines, coupled with the inherent instability of tetrazines or DHTz themselves. . . clearly the author’s system will suffer from the same challenges and unless the authors do a head to head comparison of stability, this statement be removed. I also will point out that the references cited don’t necessarily support the authors claim, particularly that of the instability of DHTz’s which are actually very stable structures in comparison to tetrazines.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
• What are the noteworthy results?
In this manuscript, Guo, Zheng and coworkers describe a click-to-release reaction involving mono-alkyl-hydroxylamines and cyclooctynes. The method builds on retro-Cope Elimination work from the labs of Kim, with modification of using a secondary (rather than tertiary) hydroxylamine in combination with a cyclooctyne bearing a propargylic leaving group. The cycloaddition is efficient provided sufficient concentrations of reactants, and release kinetics are rapid. The authors characterize the kinetics (rates in the range k2 ~10E1), and demonstrate the release of varied payloads. Reactions are demonstrated to be successful in vivo and under cell culture conditions.

• Will the work be of significance to the field and related fields? How does it compare to the established literature? If the work is not original, please provide relevant references.
While the reaction chemistry is related to prior art, the addition of release chemistry to the retro-Cope reaction is an intriguing addition that will be appreciated by the chemical biology community.

Kinetics are a challenge for the described work, as they lag significantly behind the click-to-release methodologies involving TCO and tetrazine, and we are left wondering what niche this new method will find for the field. The cellular experiments in Figure 5 are described as “confirming intracellular activation”, but there is no evidence to whether the reactants are even cell permeable, as reactions could take place extracellularly and deliver payload which subsequently becomes internalized.
Such “on cell” demonstrations are of limited value relative to demonstrations where one reactant is clearly localized to a cellular target (e.g. via a covalent bond). In Figure 6, while it can be concluded that disulfide reduction takes place intracellularly, there is no way to conclude that the cycloaddition takes place inside a cell. For the in vivo experiment described in Fig 6c, there is no evidence that uncaging takes place with spatial control. The uncaging could take place anywhere within the animal, followed by enhanced retention in cancerous tissue. This is a known effect for other dyes used in NIR imaging (review: PMC10827512).

In vivo studies appear to indicate that the combination of 6a + 5c is more effective than doxirubicin itself. This potentially significant finding warrants additional study to higher statistical significance. The concluding statement from this section that “These in vivo findings confirm that our GSH-triggered bioorthogonal click–release strategy effectively activates the prodrug within the tumor microenvironment, leading to targeted cancer therapy with enhanced efficacy and minimal systemic toxicity” needs to be reconsidered, as there is no evidence that the click reaction takes place at the tumor.

Finally, the authors use light to uncage a hydroxylamine (6b), which can then be used to uncage a fluorophore in vitro, or tetracaine on the plantar surface of rat paws. These uncaging experiments are successful, but it is unclear why the authors pursue a double uncaging experiment, when tetracaine could have just been as easily have been directly caged and photouncaged.

Summary: I find this to be interesting chemistry. Applications are limited by modest reaction rates that are going to limit in vivo and cellular applications. Biological experiments were performed “on cells” and in vivo at high concentrations without hard evidence for spatial control.

• Does the work support the conclusions and claims, or is additional evidence needed?
yes

• Are there any flaws in the data analysis, interpretation and conclusions? Do these prohibit publication or require revision?
The major flaw, described above, relates to the interpretation of spatial control.

• Is the methodology sound? Does the work meet the expected standards in your field?
yes

• Is there enough detail provided in the methods for the work to be reproduced?
yes

DISCUSSION
Over the past decade, significant advances have been made in the development of
click–release chemistries for controlled drug delivery. However, conventional
platforms remain limited by their inherent “always-on” reactivity, which limits
spatiotemporal precision and increases the risk of off-target activation. In this study,
we introduce a distinct bioorthogonal bond-cleavage strategy based on the reaction
between mono-alkyl- hydroxylamine and COT derivatives. By structurally masking the
hydroxylamine moiety with stimuli-responsive groups, we achieved conditional
activation triggered by either endogenous signals (e.g., elevated GSH) or exogenous
stimuli (e.g., light), establishing a versatile and modular platform for spatiotemporally
regulated bioorthogonal activation.
The system was validated across multiple in vivo models. In the tumor-targeted
prodrug delivery study, we demonstrated GSH-triggered activation within the tumor
microenvironment, leading to enhanced doxorubicin accumulation and reduced
systemic exposure, as confirmed by UPLC-MS based pharmacokinetic analyses. In the
local anesthesia model, we showed that photocaged hydroxylamine (6b) enabled
repeatable, on-demand drug release when activated by light, without observable
toxicity. This two-pronged validation highlights the platform’s dual capability for both
endogenous- and exogenous-triggered therapeutic control.
Despite these promising results, several challenges remain. First, the reaction
kinetics of the COT/hydroxylamine system are slower than those of fast Tz/TCO system.
Future efforts will focus on modifying the electronic and steric properties of the COT
scaffold or linkers to accelerate release rates and broaden biological applicability.
Second, potential side reactivity of strained alkynes with thiols is a well-known issue.
Our system addresses this through rational COT design: the incorporation of a
propargylic electron-withdrawing group reduces radical stability and minimizes
thiol–yne reactivity. This was confirmed through comprehensive nucleophile stability
testing, where 4b exhibited excellent resistance to degradation by GSH and cysteine,
unlike BCN 1a. Third, although hydroxylamine can be reactive in biological systems,
our prodrug design ensures that the masked form is biologically inert until activated.
Nonetheless, long-term safety and biodistribution studies of hydroxylamine derivatives
remain important directions for translational development.
Notably, the dual-step design of our system also enables spatiotemporal hierarchy
and amplification. For example, in the local anesthesia model, light-triggered release
of the reactive hydroxylamine enabled localized, confined activation of the downstream
COT-prodrug. Looking forward, this modular activation strategy may be integrated
with bioorthogonal cascade amplification systems—such as those previously developed
by our group ( Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 64, e202414246 (2025))—wherein a limited
exogenous trigger can initiate a self-propagating activation loop for enhanced signal
or drug release in deep or heterogeneous tissues.

5616-5621 (2021)) enables future multiplexed therapeutic or diagnostic strategies in
complex biological settings. Together with recent reports of dual-click systems in vivo
(Staudinger and Tz/TCO) (Nat. Biomed. Eng. 9, 686–699 (2025)), our approach
reinforces the importance of chemically diverse, orthogonal activation platforms for
next-generation chemical biology and drug delivery.
In summary, we have developed a modular and biocompatible click–release system
based on mono-alkyl- hydroxylamine and COT derivatives, capable of spatiotemporally
controlled drug activation through either endogenous or exogenous triggers. This
platform was validated in both tumor-targeted prodrug therapy and light-activated
local anesthesia models, demonstrating strong in vivo efficacy, minimal off-target
toxicity, and evidence of spatially localized activation. Pharmacokinetic studies
confirmed that drug release occurs preferentially at the tumor site, supporting the
premise of bioorthogonal activation within a physiological context.
While the current system operates with slower kinetics than mainstream Tz/TCO
platforms, its tunable controllability, bioorthogonality, and favorable safety profile
provide a strong foundation for therapeutic applications where temporal precision and
stimulus-responsiveness are prioritized. Future directions will focus on enhancing
reaction kinetics, integrating amplification mechanisms, and conducting extended
efficacy and safety evaluations across clinically relevant models. This work thus lays a
versatile chemical foundation for next-generation, conditionally activated drug
delivery systems.

achieve the spatiotemporal control of the payload release, the authors caged the amino
group on the alkylhydroxylamine so that the self-elimination can be controlled by the
on-demand uncaging the hydroxylamino group. You see, what's the adavantage of the
spationally controllable click-release systeme utilizing the mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine
and cyclooctyne over the bioorthogonal click and release reactions employing N,N-
dialkylenamine N-oxides and diboron reagents or reducing conditons?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful question regarding the advantage of
our spatiotemporally controllable click-release platform based on mono-alkyl-
hydroxylamine and cyclooctyne over previously reported bioorthogonal release systems
involving N,N-dialkyl-enamine N-oxides triggered by reductants such as diboron
reagents. Indeed, we acknowledge the excellent foundational work on enamine N-oxide-
based release systems (e.g., Chem 2022, 8, 2260–2277; ACS Cent. Sci. 2021, 7, 631–
640), which offer redox-responsive activation via selective reduction. Building on Kim's
group seminal work, our research broadens the applications of hydroxylamine-COT
click chemistry, enhancing the existing mechanistic understanding and enabling a
wider range of functionalities. Specifically, our system introduces a fundamentally
distinct and advantageous strategy for spatiotemporal control, enabled by the following
key innovations:
1. Intrinsically Triggerable Click–Release Without Need for Exogenous Reducing
Agents.
Unlike N-oxide-based systems that rely on exogenous chemical triggers (e.g., diboron
reagents or reducing environments), our click–release platform employs N-alkyl-
hydroxyl-enamine intermediates that undergo spontaneous β-elimination of the payload
at the propargylic position under physiological conditions—no additional chemical
activation is required. This property simplifies in vivo applications by eliminating
reliance on systemically administered triggers, which may have limited bioavailability
or cause undesired systemic effects.
2. Modular Spatiotemporal Activation via Caging the Mono-Alkyl-Hydroxylamine.
As described in(ACS Cent. Sci. 2021, 7, 631–640), hypoxia has been utilized within
tumors to enable activation of hypoxia-responsive prodrugs and imaging agents.
However, our approach expands upon this by allowing for spatiotemporally controlled
reaction through the modular modification of the nitrogen atom of the hydroxylamine
with a variety of stimuli-responsive groups (e.g., disulfide for redox-responsiveness, o-
nitrobenzyl for photocaging), thus broadening the scope of controllable conditions. This
strategic design decouples the click reaction and subsequent release, ensuring the
active process remains dormant until specifically triggered by a selected endogenous
(e.g., high GSH) or exogenous (e.g., light) stimulus. This enables high adaptability
across a wide range of biological environment.
This dual-layered control (bioorthogonality + on-demand activation) is not easily
achievable with the N-oxide/diboron approach, where the reducing reagent is
administered systemically and lacks spatial specificity.
3. In Vivo Biocompatibility and Application Readiness.
Our system exhibits excellent biological stability and safety: Mono-alkyl-
hydroxylamine derivatives exhibited no cytotoxicity even at 1 mM concentration in
cellular environments. Co-administration in a local anesthesia model revealed no
observable toxicity or inflammation; The click partners (COT derivatives) were
demonstrated to be exceptionally stable toward biological nucleophiles (GSH, Cys),
unlike conventional strained alkynes such as BCN, which undergo thiol addition side
reactions.
These features support its safe and selective use in complex in vivo environments,
without off-target activation or byproduct generation—challenges that can limit the
practicality of some reduction-based systems in living organisms.
4. Versatility for Multiplexed and Precision Therapy
Our platform’s orthogonality to Tz/TCO systems (as validated in prior studies, JACS
2021, 143, 5616–5621) and its compatibility with dual activation schemes (e.g., GSH
+ light) make it highly attractive for multiplexed applications, such as:
 Spatiotemporally controlled dual-drug delivery in vivo, mediated by dual click-release systems with orthogonal activation.
 Integration into pretargeted antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs), where localized
activation dramatically improves therapeutic indices.
This modular and adaptable nature is more difficult to achieve with N-oxide systems
that depend on global reductive environments or the pharmacokinetics of the reducing
agents.
In summary, our mono-alkyl-hydroxylamine/COT-based click–release system offers:
 Inherently spontaneous release after click reaction (no additional chemistry
required),
 Precise temporal and spatial control via various conditional uncaging,
 Operational simplicity and modularity for versatile therapeutic designs.
These features distinguish our approach from prior art and, we believe, provide a
valuable and practical advance in the field of bioorthogonal chemistry and drug
delivery. We have elaborated on these advantages throughout the revised manuscript,
particularly in the Discussion section, where we provide a detailed comparison
between our system and existing N-oxide-based reductive click–release strategies. By

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In a prior evaluation of this manuscript, it was noted that the manuscript describes interesting chemistry, but applications are limited by modest reaction rates that will hinder in vivo and cellular applications. It was further noted that some biological experiments were performed “on cells” while others were conducted in vivo at high concentrations without hard evidence for spatial control. In this revised manuscript, the authors have partially addressed some of the concerns raised previously but some questions remain.

In their response, they do provide a brief comment on the rate limitation of the rate constant, but further opine that reaction kinetics alone do not dictate the utility of a bioorthogonal reaction, especially in in vivo contexts where factors such as stability, biocompatibility, and controllability are equally, if not more, critical.”

While it is of course true that rate constant is not the only important parameter, it is hard to argue that it is not a critical parameter, as bioorthogonal chemistry requiring millimolar concentrations of reagents introduces a host of limitations (toxicity, background, washout in cellular experiments, clearance in animal experiments, etc).

In response to a comment that it was not shown that reactions are taking place intracellularly, the authors used a triphenylphosphonium-conjugated hydroxylamine derivative (compound 2j) to target the group to the mitochondria. While this experiment suggests that the reaction occurs intracellularly, the authors should note that TPP targeting is non-covalent and reversible, allowing for an extracellular reaction to be possible. In general, the use of covalent intracellular ligands (e.g., SnapTag or HaloTag) is necessary to prove intracellular reactivity. The images provided in the supporting information to support this experiment are of low resolution; higher-resolution images should be provided.

In the prior review, it was noted that there was insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the click reaction uncages the prodrug at the tumor. In response, the authors carried out biodistribution comparing the prodrug system (6a + 5c) versus free doxorubicin. The authors describe the findings as “strong pharmacokinetic evidence that the bioorthogonal click–release reaction predominantly occurs at the tumor site”, but the data require further interpretation. In Fig S21, slightly higher accumulation is actually observed for the Dox control at 2 hours, and there is no statistical difference at 24 h. At 4 and 8 hours, a statistical difference is observed (p value *), although the difference in tumor uptake is relatively modest. My view of these data is that Dox accumulation is comparable for the uncaging system vs the control, with the benefit of lower background in the release system.

Finally, it was noted that photochemical uncaging experiments were successful; however, it is unclear why the authors pursued a double uncaging experiment in animals when tetracaine could have been directly photouncaged more easily. The authors discuss the need to “(1) Decouple activation from payload structure and (2) provide spatiotemporal hierarchy and amplification... This separation between trigger and release enables precise spatial targeting and repeatable, on-demand drug activation, as demonstrated in our local anesthesia model.” I do not find either of these responses especially compelling. Coupling photochemistry to a kinetically slow seems disadvantaged relative to a simple photochemical uncaging, and more reagents need to be synthesized in the dual uncaging approach. The authors point to signal amplification, as they have described in Angew. Chem. for dihydrotetrazine/TCO chemistry, but it is not clear how that will apply here, and the aforementioned kinetic limitations would seem to counter any advantages for the present system.

As before, I find this to be an interesting study, but one that is ultimately more limited than current art in the field.

disadvantaged relative to a simple photochemical uncaging, and more reagents need to
be synthesized in the dual uncaging approach. The authors point to signal amplification,
as they have described in Angew. Chem. for dihydrotetrazine/TCO chemistry, but it is
not clear how that will apply here, and the aforementioned kinetic limitations would
seem to counter any advantages for the present system.
As before, I find this to be an interesting study, but one that is ultimately more limited
than current art in the field.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful comments and the opportunity to
clarify our rationale.
Our work primarily aims to introduce a new controllable click-release chemistry
and demonstrate its in vivo feasibility through two representative models: an
endogenous-triggered tumor therapy and an exogenous-triggered local anesthesia. We
agree that if the goal were solely controllable anesthetic release, direct photouncaging
would suffice. However, the anesthesia study was designed as a proof-of-concept to
demonstrate that this chemistry can be externally actuated in living tissue, decoupling
the trigger from the payload structure and illustrating its generality across application
contexts.
The dual uncaging design enables platform modularity and precise control. By
separating the trigger from the payload, one can readily adapt the same chemistry to
different external stimuli (light, redox, enzymatic), while maintaining consistent
pharmacological properties. This architecture also allows hierarchical spatiotemporal
control, where the external stimulus defines the activation site and the click step governs
the release profile, enhancing selectivity and minimizing off-target effects.
Regarding kinetics, we fully acknowledge their importance. The current rate is
sufficient for controlled in vivo release, and we explicitly state in the revised
Discussion that future optimization to improve the second-order rate constant will be pursued.
Finally, our system is complementary to the tetrazine/TCO pair rather than an
optimization of it. Unlike tetrazines, which are unstable in highly reducing
environments (e.g., high GSH) (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2022, 144, 18, 8171–8177) (Angew.
Chem. Int. Ed. 2019, 58, 9043), our hydroxylamine-based chemistry remains stable and
even benefits from GSH (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2021, 143, 15, 5616–5621), making it
advantageous in reductive tumor microenvironments. These results collectively
establish the feasibility and versatility of this new click-release platform and highlight
directions for further development.
The corresponding revision has been made in the Discussion section as follows:
Critically, our system serves as a complementary alternative to the established Tz/TCO
pair, founded on a fundamentally different mechanism and unique operational
profile. Unlike tetrazines, which suffer from instability in highly reducing environments such
as those with high GSH concentrations56,57, our hydroxylamine-based chemistry exhibits
stability and even benefits from GSH48. This inherent advantage positions our platform as
highly suitable for deployment in reductive tumor microenvironments.
